query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

proposals.intervention: Tailor the microstructure by comparison of a fully homogenized (solution‐annealed) sample versus one aged at 700 °C to induce controlled nanoscale Ta/Zr-rich precipitates
proposals.conditions: Test samples in tensile creep at 1250 °C, measure elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and perform thermal expansion tests between 900–1100 K
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation (or absence) of nanoscale precipitates that possess thermal expansion coefficients different from the matrix
proposals.mechanism: The precipitates act as internal stress generators via thermal expansion mismatch with the matrix; in the aged state, differential expansion at the precipitate/matrix interface creates residual thermal stresses that alter dislocation mobility, elevate creep resistance, and modify the thermoelastic response
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogenized baseline, the aged alloy will exhibit higher apparent yield strength in creep tests, a shift in elastic modulus temperature dependence, and measurable local lattice strain gradients; the magnitude of these effects should correlate with the precipitate density
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This unified hypothesis links the earlier disparate findings (tensile creep, hardness changes, elastic modulus shifts, and aging-induced hardening) by invoking a common precursor—thermal expansion mismatch at heterophase boundaries—thus explaining both mechanical and thermoelastic behavior

proposals.intervention: Implement controlled deformation processing by varying cold rolling reductions (e.g., 0%, 50%, 75%) followed by a standardized thermal annealing step to partially recover and stabilize dislocation structures
proposals.conditions: Conduct comparative measurements at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1250 °C, alongside in situ elastic modulus and thermal expansion measurements between 293 K and 1100 K
proposals.structural_mediator: Variation in dislocation density and substructure (cell walls) that interact with inherent lattice distortions and localized thermal expansion anisotropy
proposals.mechanism: High dislocation densities introduced during cold rolling become stabilized upon annealing, and the resulting heterogeneous dislocation networks create localized regions with different effective thermal expansion coefficients. These in turn generate internal stresses during thermal cycling that modulate both creep and elastic responses
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with heavier cold rolling (higher dislocation density) will show enhanced hardening and altered elastic modulus behavior at high temperatures relative to minimally deformed controls; differences in measured thermal expansion coefficients at the mesoscale will be evident
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By linking deformation-induced structures with temperature-dependent mechanical properties, this strategy tests if dislocation-mediated internal stresses (augmented by thermal expansion mismatch) can coherently explain stress–strain as well as thermoelastic anomalies

proposals.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA versus a modified alloy (e.g., HfNbTaTi) with reduced Zr content
proposals.intervention: Perform a compositional comparison by fabricating the standard five-element HEA and a four-element variant with lower thermal-expansion mismatch (removing Zr), then subject both to identical thermal and mechanical testing
proposals.conditions: Execute tensile creep tests at 1250 °C, elastic modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K, and thermal expansion tests from 900–1100 K under identical processing and loading conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Intrinsic lattice distortion and compositional segregation which influence local thermal expansion and residual stress fields
proposals.mechanism: The presence of Zr, known to induce larger lattice distortions and higher thermal expansion, creates local mismatches when combined with the other refractory elements. By reducing Zr, the alloy’s overall thermal mismatch is diminished, leading to more uniform stress distributions and altered dislocation dynamics
proposals.predicted_outcome: The modified (Zr-reduced) alloy should display a more homogeneous elastic modulus response and reduced creep strength anomalies compared to the baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy; specifically, a less pronounced variation in thermoelastic behavior will be observed
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This controlled compositional study isolates the effect of thermal expansion mismatch originating from elemental contributions, thereby testing if the unresolved behavior stems from such mismatch-induced internal stresses

proposals.intervention: Utilize in situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction during mechanical testing to spatially resolve lattice strain evolution under controlled thermal cycling and loading conditions
proposals.conditions: Perform simultaneous tensile creep tests at 1250 °C and elastic modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K while recording diffraction patterns; compare results under uniform heating and under imposed thermal gradients simulating composite solidification conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Spatial heterogeneity in lattice strain and phase-specific thermal expansion, arising from subtle compositional fluctuations
proposals.mechanism: Local variations in lattice parameters due to compositional microsegregation lead to differential thermal expansion during heating. These lattice strain gradients produce internal stresses that alter both the stress–strain response and thermoelastic properties; the in situ diffraction will reveal how these internal strains evolve with temperature and loading
proposals.predicted_outcome: A spatially resolved pattern of lattice strains will be observed, with regions showing higher residual stresses correlating with previously identified microstructural heterogeneities. Under thermal gradients, enhanced dislocation activity and anomalous elastic responses should be detected relative to uniform heating conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly probes the central hypothesis that internal thermal stress fields, generated by thermal expansion mismatches at the microscale, govern the alloy’s mechanical and thermoelastic behavior. It provides a clear, falsifiable link between lattice-scale behavior and macroscopic properties
